title: Indo-European migrations
summary: Ancient DNA shows a massive migration from the Eurasian steppe into Central Europe. People of the Corded Ware culture in Germany traced about 75% of their ancestry to the Yamnaya, steppe herders dated to about 3300 to 2700 BC. The migration, about 4,500 years ago, was a source for at least some Indo-European languages in Europe, according to the authors of this study.

uncertainty.note: Haak et al. (2015) sample Yamnaya pastoralists from ∼3300–2700 BC and identify massive gene flow into the Corded Ware complex around 2500 BC, persisting in Central Europe until at least 3,000 years ago; Max Planck Institute notes around 75% of Corded Ware ancestry derived from Yamnaya-related steppe pastoralists.

as_recorded.value: Massive migration from the steppe was a source for Indo-European languages in Europe
Corded Ware people from Germany traced 75% of their ancestry to the Yamnaya, documenting a massive migration into the heartland of Europe from its eastern periphery.
around 75% of the ancestry of the Corded Ware people in Germany came from a population related to the Yamnaya people who were steppe pastoralists from Russia expanding westwards

where.modern_name: Eurasian steppe; stand-in pin at Samara, Russia
where.historical_name: Pontic-Caspian steppe zone between the Dnieper and Volga rivers (Early Bronze Age Yamnaya pit-grave horizon; no formal polities)

importance.justification: The steppe migrations disseminated the Indo-European language family across Europe and large parts of Asia and permanently restructured the genetic ancestry of European populations.

related.because: Subsequent eastward and southward branches of steppe pastoralists carried Indo-Iranian languages and chariot technologies into Central and South Asia.

sources.title: Massive migration from the steppe was a source for Indo-European languages in Europe (Nature 522:207–211)

reviewer_note: The link between genes and languages is an inference. This covers the move into Europe only, not the whole Indo-European spread. The pin is a stand-in on the steppe.
